2021: planned retirement (March) is delayed, and after an outage linked to manual rotation, rotation stops entirely. Nothing alerts on the key's age. The CSRB does not give the month rotation stopped.
May and June 2023: forged tokens open enterprise mailboxes. State detects on 15 June; Microsoft invalidates the key on 24 June. Widths of the short blocks are widened to be visible.
March 2024: the CSRB report. How the key was stolen is still unknown.

blocks.md:
**The crash dump that was not found.** In September 2023 Microsoft published a blog saying the most probable path was a 2021 crash dump, a snapshot of a crashed process's memory, that contained the key and was moved out of the isolated signing environment. The CSRB reports that Microsoft soon realised it had found "no evidence of a crash dump containing the 2016 MSA key material", and corrected the blog on 12 March 2024. As of the report, "Microsoft does not know how or when Storm-0558 obtained the signing key."

Whether or not that path was the real one, it is a real class of leak: any key that exists in ordinary process memory can end up in dumps, core files, swap and debugging tools. That is the argument for keeping signing keys inside an HSM, where no process ever holds the bytes.

**The CSRB's best practices for cloud providers**, each one a lesson in this course: "automated regular key rotation" (lesson 12); "storage of keys in segmented and isolated key systems (e.g., hardware security modules [HSMs] or similar)" (lesson 10); "limiting scope of keys (e.g., to individual customers in some cases)" (lesson 10's one key per application and purpose); "use of stateful token validation" (checking tokens against a record of what was actually issued); detection of forged tokens; and "tokens bound to particular operations or sessions rather than broad bearer tokens" (lesson 1's bearer problem).

The deepest lesson is the outage. Manual rotation broke production once, so rotation stopped. The fix is not braver humans but rotation that is automatic, overlapping and rehearsed, so it can run every time.

A signing key's real lifetime is not what the plan says but what the system enforces. Enforce expiry in code, alert on key age, and treat "we paused rotation" as a security incident with an owner and a deadline.

Defender view. Detect: log the key id (kid) of every accepted token and alert on retired or unexpected kids. Because the 2016 key was supposed to be inactive, Microsoft's systems signed nothing with it, so every token it signed marked attacker activity. Respond: invalidate the key, then hunt for every token it signed.

blocks.question: Which single control would most directly have made the stolen 2016 key useless by 2023?
options: Automated rotation with enforced retirement, so the key stopped being trusted after its planned 2021 retirement
Longer RSA keys
Multi-factor authentication for users
Encrypting the mailboxes at rest
blocks.explain: The key was valid only because retirement was delayed and rotation stopped. MFA protects user logins, but forged tokens bypass the login entirely; key length does not help against theft; at-rest encryption does not stop an authorised-looking reader.

blocks.question: Microsoft's September 2023 blog said the key most probably leaked through a crash dump. What does the CSRB report say about that?
options: It confirmed the crash dump with logs
The key was brute-forced
An insider was identified
Microsoft found no crash dump containing the key, corrected the blog in March 2024, and still does not know how the key was obtained
blocks.explain: The Board found no evidence for the crash dump theory and criticised the delay in correcting it. The lesson for responders: say what you know, label hypotheses as hypotheses, and correct public statements quickly.

lessons.title: The end state: workload identity instead of stored secrets

blocks.md:
Every vault has a first-secret problem. To read secrets, an app must log in to the vault. With what? If the answer is a token stored in the app's config, you have moved the secret, not removed it. The OWASP Secrets Management Cheat Sheet's advice for pipelines is to "Avoid static bootstrap credentials" and use short-lived OIDC tokens with workload identity federation instead.

The way out is to let the **platform vouch for the workload**. The platform already knows which code it is running: the cloud knows which instance a request comes from, Kubernetes knows which pod and service account, the CI system knows which repository and branch. Cloud security and IAM showed the pattern for CI (OIDC to STS) and pods (IRSA). Vault accepts the same evidence: its [Kubernetes auth method](https://developer.hashicorp.com/vault/docs/auth/kubernetes) logs a pod in with its service account token, which Vault checks by asking Kubernetes' TokenReview API whether the token is genuine and current.

**SPIFFE** (the Secure Production Identity Framework for Everyone) is an open standard for doing this everywhere, not only in one cloud. Its [concepts page](https://spiffe.io/docs/latest/spiffe-about/spiffe-concepts/) defines:

- A **SPIFFE ID**: a URI (Uniform Resource Identifier) naming a workload, such as `spiffe://acme.com/billing/payments`: a **trust domain** (the trust root, such as an organisation) plus a path.
- An **SVID** (SPIFFE Verifiable Identity Document): the document proving that ID: an X.509 certificate (the certificate format TLS uses) or a JWT. X.509-SVIDs are preferred: JWTs "are susceptible to replay attacks".
- The **Workload API**: a local endpoint handing a workload its SVID and private key. It "does not require that a calling workload have any knowledge of its own identity, or possess any authentication token", so "your application need not co-deploy any authentication secrets". And "all private keys (and corresponding certificates) are short lived, rotated frequently and automatically".

SPIRE (SPIFFE Runtime Environment) attests workloads and issues SVIDs.

blocks.title: Two services authenticate with no stored secret (SPIFFE)

scenes.caption: The agent on each node first proves to the server which machine it is (node attestation). No password is installed by hand.

The payments workload starts and calls the local Workload API. The agent identifies the calling process from what the platform reports about it (workload attestation), not from anything the process presents.

The agent returns a short-lived X.509-SVID for spiffe://acme.com/billing/payments, its private key and the trust bundle (the CA certificates used to check other SVIDs). Before it expires, a fresh one arrives automatically.

Payments calls the ledger over mTLS (mutual TLS: both sides present certificates). Each side checks the other's SVID against the trust bundle and authorizes by SPIFFE ID. Nothing in either service's config could be copied and reused for long.
The same identity can be exchanged for cloud credentials or Vault access through OIDC federation, so even third-party secrets are fetched by identity, not by a stored token.

blocks.md:
**A ladder, not a switch.** Real systems climb in steps, and each step shrinks one factor from lesson 1:

1. Hard-coded in source (CWE-798): every copy of the code is a copy of the key.
2. Injected at runtime from config or environment: out of git, still long-lived.
3. Static secret in a vault: one copy, access-controlled, audited, rotatable.
4. Dynamic secret from a vault: unique per consumer, expires on its own.
5. Workload identity: no stored secret; short-lived credentials issued to proven identities.

Some secrets never reach step 5: an API key for a SaaS product that offers no federation, a root CA key, an HSM PIN. Keep those in a vault, rotate them, scan for them, and protect the very top with HSMs and ceremonies.
The best secret is one that does not exist at rest. Where one must exist, make it short-lived, unique to one consumer, held in one audited place and rotated automatically with overlap.

Defender view. Detect: log every SVID or token issuance with the identity it was issued to; alert on a workload asking for an identity it never had, on attestation failures, and on identities used from unexpected nodes. Respond: revoke the registration entry, and because SVIDs are short-lived, a stolen one expires soon on its own.

blocks.question: A team moves an app's database password from its Git repository into a Vault secret, but the app logs in to Vault with a long-lived Vault token stored in its config file. What has improved and what has not?
options: Nothing improved
Everything is solved because Vault encrypts its storage
The password is out of Git, audited and rotatable, but the bootstrap token is now the long-lived secret to protect; platform identity would remove it
It is worse because Vault is a single point of failure
blocks.explain: Moving to a vault shrinks copies and adds audit and rotation, but the first secret just moved. Logging in with platform identity (Kubernetes, cloud or SPIFFE) removes the stored bootstrap token.

blocks.question: Why does SPIFFE prefer X.509-SVIDs over JWT-SVIDs where possible?
options: JWTs cannot carry a SPIFFE ID
A JWT captured in transit can be replayed to impersonate the workload, while an X.509-SVID proves possession of a private key in a TLS handshake
X.509 certificates never expire
JWTs need a vault
blocks.explain: The SPIFFE concepts page says tokens are susceptible to replay; with X.509 the private key never travels. JWT-SVIDs still exist for cases such as an application-layer (L7) proxy sitting between workloads.

blocks.md:
**Practise legally.** Only test systems you own or have written permission to test. Good places for this course:

- [OWASP WrongSecrets](https://github.com/OWASP/wrongsecrets): a deliberately vulnerable app "packed with real life examples of how to not store secrets", from Docker images to Kubernetes, Vault and cloud setups. Find the secrets, then fix how each is stored.
- [Vault tutorials](https://developer.hashicorp.com/vault/tutorials/get-started): run a dev server on your laptop and try policies, dynamic database credentials and transit.
- [flAWS](http://flaws.cloud/) and [flAWS 2](http://flaws2.cloud/): AWS levels about leaked keys and their consequences, with a defender path.
- [CyLab Security Academy](https://cylabacademy.org/): Carnegie Mellon's free practice platform, including cryptography challenges.

Run gitleaks or TruffleHog against your own repositories' full history, and only against repositories you own.
